title: Indirect and Reported Questions
summary: Use statement word order inside indirect questions, keep or remove do-support appropriately, introduce yes/no information with if or whether, and report what someone asked using the correct perspective and tense.
learningObjectives: Turn direct wh-questions into polite embedded questions with statement word order.
Remove direct-question do-support when building embedded present-simple or past-simple clauses.
Use if or whether to embed yes/no questions in both enquiries and reports.
Report wh-questions and yes/no questions with appropriate pronouns and past reporting tenses.

explanation.heading: Use normal statement order inside an indirect question
explanation.body: A question can be part of another sentence after phrases such as Could you tell me, Do you know, I wonder or I can’t remember. Within that embedded clause, put the subject before the verb, even though the whole sentence may still ask for information. Only the outer question, if there is one, uses direct-question inversion.
explanation.example: Could you tell me where the conference room is?

explanation.heading: Remove unnecessary do, does and did inside the clause
explanation.body: Do, does and did help form direct simple-tense questions but do not normally remain when those questions become embedded clauses. Use the correctly inflected main verb with ordinary subject–verb order: where she works or why they left, not where does she work or why did they leave.
explanation.example: I wonder why the courier arrived so late.

explanation.heading: Keep existing auxiliaries after the embedded subject
explanation.body: For embedded questions involving can, will, have or be, keep the auxiliary but put it after the embedded subject: how long she has been waiting or where they can park. The outer expression may itself be a direct question and still needs its own word order.
explanation.example: Do you know when the new timetable will be published?

explanation.heading: Use if or whether for yes/no information
explanation.body: A direct yes/no question has no what or where to introduce its embedded form. Instead, use if or whether after know, ask, wonder or similar expressions. Both can convey uncertainty about whether a statement is true; neither requires an extra do-support verb inside the clause.
explanation.example: I don’t know whether the final presentation has started.

explanation.heading: Report wh-questions using asked and a clause
explanation.body: When retelling a past question, start with a reporting verb such as asked or wanted to know, then use question word + subject + verb. Backshift is common after a past reporting verb, and first- or second-person pronouns must reflect who asked and answered. A reported question normally ends with a full stop, not a question mark.
explanation.example: The receptionist asked me where I was staying.

explanation.heading: Report yes/no questions and keep the original meaning
explanation.body: A question like Are you free tomorrow? becomes asked if/whether I was free the next day when the reporter is the original listener. The reporting verb identifies the earlier speech; the if/whether clause is not a fresh direct question. Choose time references and tenses that remain true to the original situation.
explanation.example: My tutor asked whether I had received the instructions.

comparisons.title: A direct question and an embedded question

left.label: Direct
left.note: The auxiliary is precedes the subject in a direct enquiry.

right.label: Embedded
right.example: Could you tell me where the registration desk is?
right.note: The embedded clause has the subject before is.

comparisons.title: Do-support and a simple embedded clause

left.label: Direct with do-support
left.example: Why did the client cancel the appointment?
left.note: Did helps form the direct past-simple question.

right.label: Embedded without did
right.example: I wonder why the client cancelled the appointment.
right.note: The embedded clause uses cancelled directly, without did.

comparisons.title: Reporting a wh-question and a yes/no question

left.label: Wh-question
left.example: The interviewer asked how I travelled to work.
left.note: How introduces a reported question about manner.

right.label: Yes/no question
right.example: The interviewer asked whether I travelled to work by train.
right.note: Whether introduces a reported question with two possible truth values.

examples.sentence: Could you explain why the connection keeps dropping?
examples.note: Only the main question uses inversion; why the connection keeps dropping has statement order.

examples.sentence: I don’t remember what time the guests arrived.
examples.note: The embedded past-simple clause does not need did.

examples.sentence: Do you know how much the repairs will cost?
examples.note: Will follows the subject the repairs in the embedded clause.

examples.sentence: We are not sure if the restaurant is open on Mondays.
examples.note: If introduces a yes/no uncertainty in normal clause order.

examples.sentence: The guide asked us why we had chosen the longer route.
examples.note: The reported wh-question uses subject–verb order and a past perfect reporting form.

examples.sentence: She wanted to know whether I could work on Saturdays.
examples.note: Whether introduces a reported yes/no question; could reports earlier can.

commonMistakes.incorrect: Can you tell me where is the nearest exit?
commonMistakes.correct: Can you tell me where the nearest exit is?
commonMistakes.why: Inside the embedded question, the subject must precede is.

commonMistakes.incorrect: I wonder what did the manager decide.
commonMistakes.correct: I wonder what the manager decided.
commonMistakes.why: An embedded past-simple clause uses decided without question-form did.

commonMistakes.incorrect: He asked me did I have enough time.
commonMistakes.correct: He asked me if I had enough time.
commonMistakes.why: A reported yes/no question needs if or whether and ordinary clause order.

commonMistakes.incorrect: Do you know when will the results be announced?
commonMistakes.correct: Do you know when the results will be announced?
commonMistakes.why: The modal will comes after the embedded subject the results.

studyTips: Underline the outer phrase, then mark the embedded subject; place every embedded auxiliary after that subject.
Turn short direct questions into clauses after I wonder and Do you know; delete do-support when it no longer belongs.
For reported questions, check three separate changes: if/whether or wh-word, statement word order, and who I/you refers to now.

exercises.prompt: A visitor needs directions. Could you tell me where ___?
exercises.feedback: An embedded where-clause has statement order: the information desk is.

exercises.prompt: The organiser left early yesterday. I can’t remember why ___.
exercises.feedback: Inside I can’t remember why, use subject + past verb: she left early.

exercises.prompt: We are unsure about the starting time. Do you know ___ the seminar starts at nine?
exercises.feedback: Whether introduces a yes/no question about the truth of the starting time.

exercises.prompt: During yesterday’s interview, the recruiter asked me ___ the proposal.
exercises.feedback: A reported yes/no question uses if + subject + auxiliary + participle.

exercises.prompt: Ask politely where the laboratory is now. Complete: Could you tell me ___? (where / the laboratory / be). Write the embedded clause.
acceptedAnswers: where the laboratory is
exercises.feedback: The embedded where-clause uses the laboratory is, not is the laboratory.

exercises.prompt: Complete the statement about yesterday: I wonder ___ yesterday. (why / the manager / leave). Write the words between wonder and yesterday.
acceptedAnswers: why the manager left
exercises.feedback: A simple past embedded question drops did and uses the manager left.

exercises.prompt: Use the present perfect to ask whether confirmation has already arrived: We do not know ___ yet. (whether / the supplier / confirm / the order). Write the embedded clause.
acceptedAnswers: whether the supplier has confirmed the order
exercises.feedback: Whether introduces a yes/no uncertainty and has confirmed stays after the subject.

exercises.prompt: Yesterday an interviewer asked if you were available for weekend work. Report it using whether and past tense: The interviewer asked me ___. (whether / I / be / available for weekend work).
acceptedAnswers: whether I was available for weekend work
exercises.feedback: The reported question uses whether + I + was, not direct-question inversion.

exercises.prompt: Correct the sentence: Can you tell me where does the shuttle stop?
acceptedAnswers: Can you tell me where the shuttle stops?
exercises.feedback: Inside the embedded question, delete does and use the third-person present form stops.

exercises.prompt: Correct the sentence: I don’t know what time did the event finish.
acceptedAnswers: I don’t know what time the event finished.
exercises.feedback: The embedded past-simple clause takes subject + finished without did.

exercises.prompt: Correct the sentence: They asked if was I ready for the inspection.
acceptedAnswers: They asked if I was ready for the inspection.
exercises.feedback: A reported yes/no question uses if + subject + verb, not inversion.

exercises.prompt: Correct the sentence: Could you explain why does the app freeze at launch?
acceptedAnswers: Could you explain why the app freezes at launch?
exercises.feedback: The embedded why-clause needs statement word order and the singular verb freezes.

speakingExercises.prompt: Turn “Where is the nearest pharmacy?” into a polite question beginning “Could you tell me”. Keep the word nearest.
acceptedAnswers: Could you tell me where the nearest pharmacy is?
speakingExercises.feedback: In the embedded clause, the pharmacy comes before is.

speakingExercises.prompt: Turn “When does the conference begin?” into an indirect question beginning “Do you know”.
acceptedAnswers: Do you know when the conference begins?
speakingExercises.feedback: Delete direct-question does and change begin to begins in the embedded clause.

speakingExercises.prompt: Ask whether the printer is available now. Begin “Do you know whether” and use one complete question.
acceptedAnswers: Do you know whether the printer is available now?
speakingExercises.feedback: Whether introduces yes/no information; the printer is uses statement word order.

speakingExercises.prompt: Turn “Why did the visitor leave early?” into a statement beginning “I wonder”.
acceptedAnswers: I wonder why the visitor left early.
speakingExercises.feedback: The embedded clause uses left without did.

speakingExercises.prompt: Yesterday an interviewer asked you, “Do you work remotely?” Report the question. Begin “The interviewer asked me whether” and use the past simple.
acceptedAnswers: The interviewer asked me whether I worked remotely.
speakingExercises.feedback: The reported yes/no question changes you to I and work to worked.

speakingExercises.prompt: A guide asked you, “Where are you staying?” Report the question starting “The guide asked me”. Use the past continuous.
acceptedAnswers: The guide asked me where I was staying.
speakingExercises.feedback: Where I was staying is embedded word order; was staying reports are staying.

speakingExercises.prompt: Say exactly two sentences in this order. First turn “What time does the shipment arrive?” into a question beginning “Could you tell me”. Second report a friend’s question “Where are you waiting?” beginning “My friend asked me” and using the past continuous.
acceptedAnswers: Could you tell me what time the shipment arrives? My friend asked me where I was waiting.
speakingExercises.feedback: Arrives needs no does inside the first question; was waiting uses statement order in the reported question.

speakingExercises.prompt: Turn “How much will the repair cost?” into one statement starting “I would like to know”. Keep will.
acceptedAnswers: I would like to know how much the repair will cost.
I’d like to know how much the repair will cost.
speakingExercises.feedback: The repair precedes will within the embedded question.

listeningExercises.audioText: Could you tell me when the next ferry leaves? I must be at the harbour before noon.
listeningExercises.prompt: What information does the speaker need?
choices: The name of the ferry captain.
listeningExercises.feedback: When the next ferry leaves asks for a departure time.

listeningExercises.audioText: I asked whether the library was open on Sunday, and the librarian said it would be closed.
choices: The library would be closed on Sunday.
The librarian did not know the hours.
listeningExercises.feedback: The answer would be closed directly settles the earlier whether-question.

listeningExercises.audioText: I don’t know where the spare key is. Perhaps it is with the caretaker.
listeningExercises.prompt: Type the five-word embedded question immediately after “know”.
acceptedAnswers: where the spare key is
listeningExercises.feedback: Where the spare key is has the subject before the auxiliary is.

listeningExercises.audioText: The interviewer asked where I had worked before, and I told her about my job at the regional museum.
listeningExercises.feedback: The speaker names a past job at the regional museum.

listeningExercises.audioText: I wondered why the train stopped just outside the station. The announcement mentioned a signal problem.
choices: It had arrived at its destination.
listeningExercises.feedback: The announcement identifies a signal problem as the cause.

listeningExercises.audioText: Could you tell me if the workshop has moved to Thursday? No, it is still on Wednesday.
listeningExercises.prompt: When will the workshop take place?
listeningExercises.feedback: The negative answer rules out Thursday and confirms Wednesday.

listeningExercises.audioText: She asked me whether I had received the invitation before the deadline.
listeningExercises.prompt: Type the four-word embedded phrase immediately after “me”.
acceptedAnswers: whether I had received
listeningExercises.feedback: Whether I had received uses normal embedded word order with the past perfect.

listeningExercises.audioText: Do you know what time the workshop starts on Friday? I need to arrange transport.
listeningExercises.prompt: Type the five-word embedded phrase immediately after “know”.
acceptedAnswers: what time the workshop starts
listeningExercises.feedback: What time the workshop starts is an embedded simple-present question without does.
